attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: Accurately captures the two checkable parts: the figure was undefined (no base period or multiplier given) and it was reported uncritically. The claims about intent and the rhetoric are rightly left out.

contract.note: Separating a generic definition from the actual calculation matches his wording ('a number that we do not know'). There is no threshold for 'meaningful scrutiny' and no set sample of outlets, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: CNBC, published before the post, repeats the investor-update figure without giving a base period or multiplier. This supports the omission claim for this one article only.
TechCrunch gives a generic definition and notes the companies may calculate differently. That partly qualifies 'without a second's hesitation', but it does not disclose the actual calculation.

reviews.rationale: Two articles from before the post confirm the figure was reported without its base period or multiplier. One added a brief comparability caveat. The original investor update was not obtained, and two outlets are not a representative sample. So the packet cannot show whether the company materials omitted the calculation, or whether coverage as a whole lacked meaningful scrutiny.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: The surrounding paragraph makes it reasonable to attribute the $11.6B figure to Anthropic. 'Never share' is rendered as 'do not disclose', which is fair. The rhetoric about reporters is rightly left out.

contract.note: Limiting 'AI companies' to standalone frontier developers, and 'share' to direct public disclosure, are reasonable readings. But neither the set of companies nor what counts as 'underlying economics' is defined, so the disclosure part depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: The S-1 (available Oct 26, before the evaluation date) reports Q2 2026 revenue of $11,555M, which rounds to $11.6B. That is the ordinary meaning of 'actual revenue', so it supports the numerical part only. It cannot speak to disclosure practice before September.

reviews.rationale: The numerical part holds: the S-1's Q2 2026 revenue rounds to $11.6B. The categorical disclosure part ('never share actual revenues or underlying economics') has no evidence in the packet. There is no survey of what the relevant companies publicly disclosed before September 1. Because one part is supported and the other is unsettled, the compound claim is unresolved, not mixed.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: Zitron says it is unclear which industries AI created, and that the wrapper companies, generously counted, employ negligible numbers. The normalised wording slightly broadens this to 'industries created by AI', but the contract correctly limits the target to wrapper or application businesses.

contract.note: The plain reading of 'negligible' (a very small share of total employment, not zero) is ordinary and fair. Q2 2026 is a period the evaluator chose for a statement about an ongoing state.

evidence.note: UK figures for 2024 cover the whole AI sector, including model developers and diversified firms. Wrong period and wrong population, so it cannot measure employment at wrapper companies.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no aggregate count of employment at wrapper or application companies, and no matching employment total to compare it against. The only item covers the broader UK AI sector in 2024, so it can neither confirm nor refute 'negligible' for the target population.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: The normalised wording drops the Walmart comparison, which the contract restores. It also narrows 'a data center' to AI data centers, which the context supports and the contract flags. 'When finished' is kept as a qualifier.

contract.note: Reading 'economic value' as net local benefit fits the surrounding argument about community benefits. Counting ongoing staffing separately from construction jobs is fair. Facility size and the line between a building and a campus remain unclear.

evidence.note: Virginia's 2024 audit finds about 50 workers at a typical facility, half of them contractors, which suggests limited staffing. It also documents tax revenue and economic benefits. But it covers data centers broadly, an earlier period, and gross rather than net benefits.
Warren release dated Oct 9, 2026 (before the evaluation date). Reports disputes over who pays infrastructure costs. It gives no figures on staffing or net value.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no representative Q2 2026 staffing data for completed AI data centers, no matched comparison with large Walmart stores, and no estimate of net local benefit. The Virginia audit suggests even lower staffing but also positive gross benefits, for a different population and period. It neither confirms nor refutes the claim.
